claims.text: Conventionally slow-cooled MnNiSi-based alloys have coarse-grained microstructures.
Conventionally slow-cooled MnNiSi-based alloys exhibit brittle fracture behavior.
Rapid melt-spinning of MnNiSi can form a nanocrystalline structure.
MnNiSi has an order-disorder transformation near approximately 600–700 °C.
Short-duration annealing near 600–700 °C can relieve residual stresses without significant grain growth.
Rapid solidification followed by controlled annealing will produce refined, uniformly distributed grain boundaries.
Refined grains and grain boundaries inhibit crack propagation in MnNiSi-based alloys.
Inhibiting crack propagation through grain refinement enhances toughness and strength.
Controlled annealing preserves the sharp, cooperative magnetic transition in melt-spun MnNiSi.
A sharp magnetic phase transition is responsible for the large magnetocaloric effect in MnNiSi-based materials.
Melt-spinning followed by controlled annealing will improve fracture toughness and strength relative to conventionally cast MnNiSi-based material.
The processed material will retain a magnetic entropy change comparable to that of conventionally cast MnNiSi-based material.
Excessive grain growth during annealing would compromise the proposed toughness improvement.
Nanostructuring may broaden the magnetic transition and thereby reduce the magnetocaloric effect.
Minor composition variations may alter the mechanical or magnetic performance of MnNiSi-based alloys.
Processing under an inert atmosphere is needed to avoid oxidation.
